Under the 2000 Regulations properly interpreted, Avalon Reeves should succeed.

1. **The correct causation test under the Regulations**

Regulation 5(1) of the Part‑time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000 provides that a part‑time worker has the right not to be treated less favourably than a comparable full‑timer “on the ground that” he is a part‑time worker.

Stone Rides argues this must be read as “solely because” he is part‑time, to mirror clause 4.1 of the Framework Agreement annexed to Directive 97/81, which uses that phrase. That is not the better view.

(a) **Text and structure of the domestic Regulations**

- The draftsman very deliberately did **not** copy the word “solely” into Reg 5(1). Instead, the familiar UK anti‑discrimination formula “on the ground that” is used.
- Regulation 5(2)(b) then provides that less favourable treatment will **not** infringe the right if it is “objectively justified on grounds other than the fact that the worker is a part‑time worker.”

That structure only makes sense if:

- Part‑time status can be **one of several operative reasons** for the treatment (otherwise there is no real role for a justification “on grounds other than” part‑time status); and
- The employer’s non‑status reasons are properly tested at the justification stage, not by hard‑wiring a “sole cause” test into Reg 5(1).

If “on the ground that” meant “solely because”, then as soon as the employer pointed to *any* additional ground (e.g. “revenue generation”), the claim would fail at stage one and the elaborate objective justification mechanism in Reg 5(2) would be largely redundant. That is not a credible reading of the scheme.

(b) **Consistency with the Directive**

Directive 97/81 sets a **minimum** level of protection. Clause 8.1 of the Framework Agreement expressly allows Member States to introduce more favourable provisions for workers. The UK is therefore free to confer **broader** protection than “solely because”; it is only prohibited from providing **less** protection.

Interpreting “on the ground that” in Reg 5(1) as “an effective or operative reason”:

- Captures all cases where treatment is “solely because” a worker is part‑time (so the minimum standard is met); and
- Goes further by catching mixed‑motive situations.

Far from conflicting with the Directive, this is entirely compatible with its text and purpose and simply reflects “gold‑plating” in favour of workers.

(c) **Analogy with other discrimination law**

In UK discrimination statutes, language such as “on grounds of” (race, sex, etc.) has consistently been interpreted to mean **an effective cause, not the only cause**. Classic authorities (e.g. *Nagarajan v London Regional Transport* in the race context) treat mixed‑motive discrimination as actionable where the protected ground is one operative factor in the decision.

There is no good reason to assume Parliament quietly adopted a radically narrower causation test for part‑time workers while using the *same* linguistic formula (“on the ground that”) it used elsewhere to denote mixed‑motive liability.

(d) **Purposive interpretation**

The object of the Regulations, in line with the Framework Agreement, is to **prevent discrimination against part‑time workers**. A “sole reason” test is trivially easy to evade: an employer can always point to a secondary rationale (cost, convenience, practice in the sector) and thereby defeat liability at the threshold.

A reading under which part‑time status must be **a real and effective reason**, but not the only reason, is:

- Faithful to the text actually chosen;
- Coherent with the internal structure of Reg 5; and
- Necessary to give the protection any meaningful practical effect.

On that basis, Reeves is right on the legal point: he need only show that his being part‑time was one effective ground for the less favourable treatment.

2. **Application to the “circuit fee”**

On the facts as you have framed them:

- All drivers pay a “circuit fee” for access to the booking system.
- Reeves contends that, in the way the scheme is designed and imposed, his **part‑time status was a real factor** in how he was treated under the scheme (e.g. in how the fee bit in practice, how the classification operated, or how different categories were drawn).
- Both sides accept that his part‑time status was a factor in the treatment; the dispute is only whether it must be the *sole* factor.

Assuming the tribunal finds, as the question posits, that:

- Reeves was disadvantaged compared with a full‑time comparator (e.g. because a flat fee weighs more heavily on someone with fewer hours and lower gross earnings, or because part‑timers were placed in a fee category that worked out worse); and
- His being part‑time was one operative reason why he ended up in that less favourable position (even if revenue‑raising and sector practice were also in play),

then, under the correct mixed‑motive test, the causation element of Reg 5(1) is satisfied.

3. **Objective justification**

Once less favourable treatment “on the ground” of being part‑time is established, Stone Rides can escape liability only if it shows objective justification under Reg 5(2):

- Legitimate aim (e.g. funding system overheads) – likely accepted.
- Appropriateness and necessity – this is where their case is weak.

A **flat, non‑pro‑rated fee** that predictably bears more heavily on part‑timers is not automatically justified just because “the sector does it” or because it raises revenue. The employer must show that:

- The particular structure of the fee (including its lack of pro rata adjustment) is reasonably necessary to achieve the aim; and
- There is no less discriminatory alternative (e.g. a percentage‑of‑booking fee or a turnover‑linked fee) that would achieve the same aim with less adverse impact on part‑time workers.

“Commercial convenience” or “this is how everyone does it” are rarely, if ever, sufficient objective justifications in discrimination-type regimes. On the limited facts given, Stone Rides does not appear to offer any cogent reason why a less burdensome, more proportionate structure could not have been adopted.

On that basis, they fail to make out the Reg 5(2) defence.

4. **Conclusion**

Properly applying the Part‑time Workers Regulations 2000:

- A claimant does **not** have to prove that part‑time status was the *only* reason for less favourable treatment; it is enough that it was one effective reason.
- On the assumed findings of fact, Reeves satisfies that test.
- Stone Rides has not, on the facts presented, shown an objective justification for the adverse impact of its fee structure on part‑time workers.

Accordingly, the court should find for Avalon Reeves.

Under the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), whether a nonsignatory like Jon Davidson can compel arbitration is governed by (1) the scope of the arbitration clause, and (2) state-law contract principles (e.g., agency, estoppel, assumption, successor liability, third‑party beneficiary). The strong federal policy favoring arbitration operates only after those contract-law predicates are met; it cannot manufacture consent where contract law would not.

I’ll walk through the key points:

---

### 1. Scope of the Arbitration Clause

The clause covers disputes “arising out of or relating to” the Gold Reserve & Lending agreement. That is among the broadest formulations courts recognize.

Under federal law, such language typically brings within arbitration:

- Tort claims (fraud, misrepresentation, breach of fiduciary duty) that are factually connected to the contract’s subject matter;  
- Statutory or extra‑contractual claims that presuppose the existence of the contractual relationship or arise from the dealings it created.

Here, the dispute is about an allegedly fraudulent tax shelter/container leasing program sold through Gold Reserve & Lending. Harper’s allegations against Davidson concern:

- His involvement “in connection with the container leasing program and related matters”;  
- His creation of entities (Fund Restoration Alliance, Tax Support Circle) that solicited more money from the same investors “under the guise of helping investors”;  
- His efforts to discourage them from pursuing lawsuits regarding that same investment.

Even if some of the alleged misconduct occurred after the original contract and via new entities, it plainly “relates to” the original investment agreement and the tax shelter scheme it implemented. Courts routinely hold that “arising out of or relating to” language reaches post‑contract conduct and follow‑on schemes that grow out of the original contractual relationship.

So as between Harper and Gold Reserve & Lending, there is no serious doubt: their dispute is within the scope of the arbitration clause.

The remaining question is whether Davidson, a nonsignatory, can invoke that clause.

---

### 2. Theories Allowing a Nonsignatory to Enforce Arbitration

Under Arthur Andersen LLP v. Carlisle and related cases, state contract and agency law determine whether a nonsignatory may enforce an arbitration agreement. Common theories include:

1. **Agency / Corporate Officer Doctrine**  
   - Officers, directors, and employees of a signatory can generally enforce an arbitration clause when:
     - The alleged misconduct occurred within the scope of their corporate roles; and
     - The claims against them are factually intertwined with arbitrable claims against the company.
   - Numerous federal appellate courts have allowed corporate officers to compel arbitration on this basis to prevent end‑runs around arbitration agreements by suing individuals instead of the company.

2. **Equitable Estoppel**  
   - A nonsignatory may compel arbitration where:
     - The signatory’s claims “rely on,” “presuppose,” or are “intimately founded in and intertwined with” the underlying contract; or  
     - The signatory alleges substantially interdependent and concerted misconduct by the nonsignatory and the signatory company, all rooted in the same underlying dealings.
   - The rationale: a plaintiff cannot simultaneously (a) invoke or rely on the contract (or its relationship) as the basis for recovery, but (b) avoid the contract’s arbitration obligation by suing an affiliated non‑signatory.

3. **Successor / Assumption**  
   - When a person or entity acquires a signatory business and effectively steps into its shoes, they may inherit the right to enforce its contracts, including arbitration clauses, if state successor‑liability or assumption principles are satisfied.

4. **Third‑Party Beneficiary / Closely Related Party**  
   - If the contract was clearly intended to benefit or protect certain non‑parties (e.g., affiliates, agents), those non‑parties can sometimes enforce the arbitration clause.

I’ll apply the most relevant of these—agency and estoppel—to the facts provided.

---

### 3. Agency / Officer Status

Facts that support agency-based enforcement:

- Davidson became an **officer, director, and eventual owner** of Gold Reserve & Lending via National Freight Consolidated.
- His involvement is described as being “in connection with the container leasing program and related matters,” which is exactly the program governed by the original contract.
- The alleged wrongful acts—discouraging litigation, purporting to be working on investors’ behalf, setting up related entities that dealt with the fallout of the tax shelter—were all undertaken in the context of the same investor relationship created by the Gold Reserve agreement.

Courts usually ask: What capacity was the individual acting in when committing the alleged misconduct? If the conduct is tightly tied to the person’s corporate role, many courts allow that officer/agent to invoke the employer’s arbitration clause.

Here:

- The complaints against Davidson are not about something entirely independent—like a personal side business totally unrelated to container leasing or tax shelters.
- They are about how he and his web of entities dealt with existing Gold Reserve investors, in a program emanating from the original contracts.

While Harper argues he used separate entities (Universal Business Services, Fund Restoration Alliance, Tax Support Circle), that alone is not dispositive. Courts look through form to substance: if the dispute stems from how an officer of the signatory interacted with customers in relation to the very investment the contract created, that is the classic situation where an agent/officer is allowed to compel arbitration to avoid eviscerating the clause by artful pleading and entity selection.

The fact that he may not have been an officer at the time of contract formation does not bar him. Arbitration rights can extend to later-appointed agents and officers so long as their relationship and conduct arise out of the contractual relationship between the signatories.

On these facts, a court applying mainstream federal and state precedents would likely find a sufficient agency/representative nexus to allow Davidson, as an officer and controlling owner of Gold Reserve & Lending, to invoke its arbitration clause for claims arising from or relating to that relationship.

---

### 4. Equitable Estoppel Analysis

Harper’s own allegations suggest that:

- The original Gold Reserve & Lending investment contracts created the investor relationship and the container leasing tax shelter structure;
- Davidson “became involved in the alleged fraudulent tax shelter scheme” that stemmed from those contracts; and
- His later entities and solicitations targeted the same investors and addressed the same losses or legal issues arising out of the original investment.

In other words, Harper’s claims against Davidson:

- Make no sense except by reference to the original investment contracts and the container leasing scheme they implemented; and  
- Allege a unified course of fraudulent conduct tied to the existence of those contracts.

Under equitable estoppel principles, that is usually enough for a nonsignatory to compel arbitration:

- Harper is effectively saying: “Because we entered these container-leasing contracts, and because of that tax shelter structure, Davidson later defrauded us in how he administered, ‘rescued,’ or manipulated our rights concerning that investment.”  
- That pattern fits the “intertwined and concerted misconduct” scenario: alleged wrongdoing by both the signatory entity (Gold Reserve & Lending) and its control person (Davidson), all in relation to the same investment program.

Harper’s attempt to characterize Davidson’s conduct as “wholly distinct” rests almost entirely on temporal and corporate-form separations (post-contract, new entities). But the substantive connection is still the original tax shelter arrangement. Courts are not persuaded merely by the existence of follow‑on entities when the dispute remains deeply rooted in the same contractual relationship and investment.

On this record, a court would likely find Harper equitably estopped from avoiding arbitration as to Davidson while relying on the factual and legal framework created by the very contracts that contain the arbitration clause.

---

### 5. Argument that Davidson’s Conduct Is “Separate” and Time-Barred from the Contract

Harper stresses:

- Davidson had “not personally signed” the original contracts;  
- He came in “after” the contracts were executed;  
- He then formed “entirely separate entities” and engaged in “independent tortious conduct” to solicit new funds and dissuade litigation.

Those arguments might defeat arbitration if:

- The later misconduct related to completely new and unrelated investments; or  
- The claims did not depend on the earlier Gold Reserve investment at all.

But that is not how the facts are framed. Davidson’s conduct was directed at the same class of investors, linked to the same tax shelter, and concerned whether and how those investors would pursue remedies for the failures of that original program. Under broad “arising out of or relating to” language, courts routinely find such follow‑on misconduct to be related to the original agreement.

Moreover:

- The FAA and case law treat timing as largely irrelevant where later events grow out of the contractual relationship.  
- The question is functional: Does the dispute have its origins in or substantial connection to the contract? Here, it plainly does.

So the “separate later fraud” argument is weaker than it first appears once the relational context is considered.

---

### 6. Effect of Default

The facts indicate: “Harper Investors obtained an order of default against Davidson, while Davidson simultaneously sought to compel arbitration.”

Default can, in some circumstances, operate as a waiver of the right to arbitrate if:

- The defendant engaged in substantial litigation conduct inconsistent with an intent to arbitrate; and  
- The plaintiff was prejudiced.

But here:

- There is no detail suggesting Davidson litigated on the merits before invoking arbitration; rather, the default appears to stem from nonresponse. Courts often set aside defaults when a party promptly asserts arbitration rights, especially under the FAA’s pro‑arbitration policy.
- Waiver is typically found where a party uses the court system to test the merits and only later switches to arbitration; we do not have that pattern here.

Given the lack of detailed prejudice and the simultaneity of the default and motion to compel, a court inclined toward arbitration would likely excuse the default, set it aside, and reach the arbitrability question—which, per the above analysis, favors Davidson.

---

### 7. Policy Considerations

Allowing Davidson to enforce the arbitration clause:

- Preserves the parties’ original expectation that disputes over this tax shelter program would be resolved in arbitration, not court;  
- Prevents plaintiffs from circumventing that agreement by suing individual officers and affiliated entities for the same conduct; and  
- Aligns with the FAA’s policy favoring arbitration once a valid agreement and applicable contract-law theory support extending it.

Denying him that right, by contrast, would encourage artful pleading: any investor could avoid arbitration with a financial firm simply by naming individual officers or newly formed affiliates, even when the core dispute plainly “relates to” the original agreement.

---

### Conclusion

Applying standard U.S. arbitration principles:

- The dispute falls within the broad “arising out of or relating to” language of the Gold Reserve & Lending contracts.
- Davidson, as an officer, director, and controlling owner of Gold Reserve & Lending and as a central actor in the same tax shelter program, can invoke the arbitration clause under both agency principles and equitable estoppel.
- The later creation of additional entities and the timing of his involvement do not break the substantive nexus between Harper’s claims and the original investment contracts.

A U.S. court applying the FAA and typical state contract doctrines should therefore allow Jon Davidson to compel arbitration.

1. Statutory framework and what must be shown

Under 26 U.S.C. § 2055(a), an estate may deduct bequests to charity if, at the decedent’s death, the value of the charitable interest is:

- exclusively for charitable purposes, and  
- “presently ascertainable” so that it can be valued.

Section 2055(e)(2) generally *disallows* deductions for “split-interest” transfers (where a noncharitable beneficiary and a charity both have interests, e.g., a life estate followed by a remainder to charity) unless the charitable remainder takes a prescribed form (CRAT, CRUT, pooled income fund, etc.).

Section 2055(e)(3) is transitional relief. It allows a deduction if:

- The original interest is a “reformable interest,” and  
- The governing instrument is timely and properly reformed, usually to conform to CRAT/CRUT requirements, without materially increasing the noncharitable benefits.

The two main disputes here are:

1. Whether Mary Winston’s trust qualifies for the more lenient “reformable interest” rules applicable to governing instruments executed before the statutory cutoff (January 1, 1979).  
2. Whether the charitable remainder was “presently ascertainable,” given the broad powers to expend for Kevin Fletcher’s benefit.

If the will is treated as a pre‑1979 governing instrument *and* the interest is “reformable” within § 2055(e)(3), the 1988 judicial reformation converting Kevin’s interest into a fixed annual amount will generally allow the charitable deduction.

---

2. Execution date: will vs. codicils

a. Text and structure of § 2055(e)(3)

Section 2055(e)(3) (in substance) distinguishes between:

- Governing instruments executed *before* a certain date (here, before January 1, 1979), which get more generous “reformable interest” treatment; and  
- Governing instruments executed *after* that date, which are subject to stricter conditions—essentially, the interest has to be the kind that would have been deductible but for technical noncompliance with the CRAT/CRUT rules.

Congress’s choice of the phrase “governing instrument (including a will) executed before [the cutoff date]” focuses on the *date of execution* of the governing instrument, not on any state‑law fiction about republication.

If Congress had wanted “any will later republished by codicil” to *lose* pre‑cutoff status, it could have said so explicitly. The prompt indicates that early legislative language tying execution to later codicils was *removed* before enactment. That is a strong indication that Congress did *not* want the common-law doctrine of republication-by-codicil to override the plain, historical execution date for this transitional rule.

b. Republication-by-codicil is a state‑law fiction, not a federal tax command

Under state wills law, a codicil is often said to “republish” a will as of the codicil date, so that, for some *state* purposes, the will is treated as made on the date of the last codicil. That doctrine serves specific functions (e.g., bringing later-acquired property under the will, dealing with omitted heirs) and is not a universal timing rule for federal tax statutes.

For federal tax, the Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasized:

- State law defines the property interests created;  
- Federal law determines the tax consequences.

Whether a will was “executed before 1979” is a simple historical fact: Mary executed the will in 1971. The 1972, 1977, and 1982 codicils were *separate* instruments, executed on their own dates, modifying the original document. They do not erase the historical reality that the will itself was executed in 1971.

Nothing in § 2055(e)(3) directs courts to import the state‑law republication fiction into the effective‑date language, and the legislative removal of codicil‑linking language cuts against doing so.

c. Statutory purpose: relief for pre‑change plans

The transition rule’s purpose was to give relief to donors whose estate plans were put in place before Congress tightened the rules on split-interest charitable gifts. Mary Winston’s basic plan—life interest to Kevin, remainder to Elmwood—was in place in 1971, just after the 1969 reforms and *well before* the 1979 cutoff for the transition rule.

Reading “executed” to mean the original 1971 will date:

- Aligns with the statute’s text,  
- Honors the apparent legislative decision not to treat codicils as re‑execution for this provision, and  
- Furthers Congress’s remedial goal of allowing old instruments to be cleaned up.

By contrast, the Government’s view—that an ordinary codicil in 1982 automatically reclassifies the entire will as “executed” in 1982 for § 2055(e)(3)—rests on a state‑law fiction that Congress did not adopt, and would arbitrarily strip transitional relief from many longstanding testamentary arrangements.

d. Conclusion on issue 1

A court should hold the relevant “governing instrument” (Mary’s will) was “executed” in 1971, before the 1979 cutoff. The more lenient pre‑cutoff “reformable interest” rules of § 2055(e)(3) therefore apply.

---

3. Ascertainability of the charitable remainder before reformation

Even under the more generous pre‑1979 rule, courts still examine whether:

- The charity is the remainderman, and  
- The noncharitable beneficiary’s rights are such that the charitable remainder is not so speculative as to be effectively illusory.

The Government’s second argument is that Kevin Fletcher’s life interest was so broad—particularly the authorization to pay for “improvements” to his Riverside home and his taxes—that the value of what would be left for Elmwood University was not “presently ascertainable” at Mary’s death.

a. Governing standard: present ascertainability and reasonable valuation

Cases like *Ithaca Trust Co. v. United States* (279 U.S. 151 (1929)) and Treasury Reg. § 20.2055-2 make clear:

- A charitable remainder is deductible if its value can be determined by “reliable actuarial principles,”  
- Even when there are invasion powers, if those powers are constrained by an objective, enforceable standard (e.g., “support,” “maintenance in accustomed manner,” “health, education, and support”), the remainder can be valued and is deductible, and  
- Only where the trustee’s power is not limited by any reasonably definite standard—e.g., to use principal as they “may deem wise and proper for the comfort, support, maintenance and/or happiness” of the beneficiary (*Merchants Nat’l Bank*), or for “pleasure, comfort and welfare” in a completely open‑ended way (*Henslee*)—is the remainder too speculative.

Thus, the crux is whether the trustee’s powers here are constrained by standards that are sufficiently objective to be valued with actuarial tools.

b. Application to Kevin Fletcher’s interest

Kevin’s benefits under the trust included:

- Fixed monthly financial payments, and  
- Payment of medical expenses, taxes, upkeep and *improvements* on a specifically identified residence, and other expenditures.

Most of those items—fixed monthly payments, medical expenses, property taxes, routine upkeep—clearly fall on the side of *actuarially estimable* obligations tied to Kevin’s life and station. Actuarial science routinely values life annuities and expected health and housing costs based on age, health, and lifestyle, just as *Ithaca Trust* approves.

The Government focuses on “improvements” and the trustee’s discretion, but:

- “Improvements” are tied to a *single, identified residence in Riverside, California*. They are not a roving mandate to fund any whim.  
- Under state trust law, the trustee owes fiduciary duties to *both* the life tenant and the charitable remainderman. That limits “improvements” to those reasonably related to Kevin’s use and enjoyment of the home (e.g., roof replacement, modest remodeling, structural repairs, perhaps accessibility modifications in light of his age), not to unlimited, extravagant rebuilding that would effectively waste Elmwood’s interest.  
- The potential future cost of such capital items, over the short remaining life expectancy of an octogenarian beneficiary, is significant but not unbounded; an actuary can assign a reasonable present value to expected improvements and capital needs.

Crucially, *Ithaca Trust* teaches that we value the charitable remainder as of the decedent’s death, based on probabilities and reasonable expectations—not on worst‑case, fanciful scenarios. The mere *theoretical* possibility that a trustee might go wild on improvements, disregarding fiduciary duties and economic reality, does not make the charitable remainder unascertainable.

Here:

- Kevin Fletcher was already in his early eighties at Mary’s death; his expected remaining lifetime is relatively short.  
- The Riverside house’s value and reasonable scope for improvements over that period are limited and can be modeled.  
- The trustee’s powers are confined to uses that are objectively linked to Kevin’s residence and well‑being—not amorphous “happiness” or “pleasure” with no external measure.

On these facts, a court should treat the remainder as “presently ascertainable” in the sense required by § 2055 and the regulations. The invasion standards are closer to the enforceable, measurable standard in *Ithaca Trust* than to the indeterminate, wholly discretionary standards in *Merchants Nat’l Bank* and *Henslee*.

c. “Other expenditures”

The prompt mentions “other expenditures” but ties them contextually to the same pattern of support‑type items. Courts construe such clauses in light of the surrounding text and the evident purpose of providing for Kevin’s reasonable support and housing, not as a license for arbitrary depletion.

When a clause is embedded among clearly support‑related categories and administered by a fiduciary who must balance Kevin’s needs against a known charitable remainder, the proper construction is that “other expenditures” must be of a similar character (ejusdem generis), further supporting actuarial estimability.

---

4. Effect of the 1988 judicial reformation under § 2055(e)(3)

Once we determine:

- The governing instrument is treated as executed in 1971 (pre‑1979), and  
- The arrangement creates a genuine, ascertainable remainder in favor of Elmwood University,

it fits within the category of “reformable interests” Congress intended to rescue via § 2055(e)(3).

The 1988 state‑court reformation:

- Converts Kevin Fletcher’s interest into a fixed annual amount—a classic charitable remainder annuity trust pattern—and  
- Does not appear to materially increase the value of the noncharitable interest compared to what Kevin could have obtained under the original discretionary standard (indeed, it likely caps the trustee’s exposure).

Section 2055(e)(3) then treats the trust, *for federal tax purposes*, as though it had been in this qualifying form at Mary Winston’s death, thereby curing the technical split‑interest problem under § 2055(e)(2).

Given that Congress enacted § 2055(e)(3) specifically so charitable remainders in pre‑cutoff instruments could be preserved by judicial reformation, denying the deduction here would run counter both to the statutory text and the remedial policy.

---

5. Conclusion

- The will is properly treated as “executed” in 1971, so the more lenient pre‑1979 transitional rules in § 2055(e)(3) apply; the 1982 codicil does not, for this federal tax purpose, convert the instrument into a post‑1979 execution.  
- Even apart from the transition rule, Kevin Fletcher’s interest—limited to specified payments, medical expenses, taxes, and reasonable upkeep and improvements on a single residence, all subject to fiduciary constraints—does not render Elmwood University’s remainder so speculative that it is not “presently ascertainable.” Actuarial valuation is feasible under established principles endorsed in *Ithaca Trust*.  
- The 1988 judicial reformation appropriately converts the trust into a qualifying split‑interest form without enhancing noncharitable benefits, fitting squarely within § 2055(e)(3).

A US court should therefore allow the estate tax charitable deduction for the remainder interest to Elmwood University.

1. **Identify the statutory framework**

- The leases and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 (LTA 1985) would, absent new legislation, allow ShelterCo to recover:
  - costs of repairs and compliance works via service charges (subject to s.19 reasonableness, consultation etc.), and  
  - associated professional and legal costs if the leases are drawn broadly enough.

- The Building Safety Act 2022 (BSA), and in particular **Schedule 8**, overlays those historic rights by:
  - defining **“relevant buildings”**, **“qualifying leases”** and **“relevant defects”**; and  
  - restricting service charges that would otherwise be contractually and statutorily recoverable.

The core question is *not* whether the BSA operates on existing contractual arrangements (it clearly does), but *how far* it goes where the landlord’s expenditure pre‑dates commencement.

---

2. **Is Lowbridge Towers within the scope of Schedule 8?**

On the given facts:

- Lowbridge Towers is over 18m and contains residential flats → it is a **“relevant building”** for Schedule 8.
- There are 32 long residential leases; at least some will, in practice, be **“qualifying leases”** (long leases of dwellings held as the leaseholder’s only or principal home, meeting the value and other conditions as at 14 February 2022).
- The building has exterior construction fire‑safety risks requiring remediation and interim safety measures → these are highly likely to be **“relevant defects”** (defects in design, workmanship or materials within the statutory period giving rise to a building safety risk due to fire spread).

Accordingly, Schedule 8 is engaged in principle.

---

3. **Does Schedule 8 apply to existing leases and historic defects?**

Yes. The statute is overtly directed at historic problems:

- A **“relevant defect”** is defined by reference to work done during a past period (30 years up to 14 February 2022). By definition, Parliament is legislating about *pre‑existing* construction.
- A **“qualifying lease”** is determined by reference to the position on 14 February 2022, a date well before commencement and after many leases were long since granted.

This structure shows a **clear and conscious legislative decision to affect existing leases and historic defects**. In Tunnicliffe v Pool BC [1992] 1 WLR 113, the Court of Appeal held that the presumption against retrospectivity yields where the statute shows a clear intention to change the legal effect of existing arrangements. Schedule 8 plainly does so.

Therefore, ShelterCo’s reliance on a broad, unqualified “no retroactivity” principle is misplaced. Any presumption is displaced by the text and scheme of the BSA itself.

---

4. **Is restricting recovery of pre‑commencement expenditure impermissibly “retrospective”?**

ShelterCo’s most attractive argument is that expenses were incurred *before* the BSA provisions came into force, so new limits on recovery would be a retroactive interference with vested contractual rights.

However, English law draws a key distinction:

- Legislation is **retrospective in the impermissible sense** if it changes the legal consequences of acts *already completed*, e.g. re‑opening judgments, undoing payments lawfully made, or imposing new liabilities for past conduct.
- By contrast, legislation is generally **not “retrospective”** merely because it affects *future enforcement* of pre‑existing contracts.

Schedule 8 does not require landlords to refund service charges already paid, nor does it set aside final determinations. Rather, it provides that **from its commencement onwards, certain service charges are simply not payable (and any contrary lease clauses are void to that extent)**.

So, in relation to costs incurred before commencement but charged or sought to be recovered *after* commencement, the BSA is operating **prospectively on the enforceability of charges**, even though the underlying expenditure is historic. That is well within orthodox legislative power and consistent with Tunnicliffe and similar authorities.

---

5. **Interaction with contractual rights and the LTA 1985**

- Before the BSA, ShelterCo’s rights were:
  - contractual (under the service charge clauses), and  
  - overlaid by sections 18–19 and 27A LTA 1985 (reasonableness and FTT scrutiny).

- The BSA is a **later, more specific statute** directed at building safety and leaseholder liability.
  - To the extent of any inconsistency, the BSA’s express limitations on service charge recovery must prevail over both the earlier statute and contractual terms (*lex posterior derogat priori*).
  - Schedule 8 explicitly declares that **lease provisions requiring prohibited charges are of no effect**. That is a direct, express curtailment of contractual rights; the court cannot prefer general contractual principles over clear statutory language.

Thus, while ShelterCo *once* had a sound contractual and LTA 1985 basis for recovery, those rights have been **partially superseded** by Schedule 8.

---

6. **Remedial and protective purpose of the BSA**

The Occupants emphasise that the BSA is **remedial, protective legislation** intended to shift the burden of historic fire‑safety defects away from leaseholders. That is borne out by:

- the Explanatory Notes and political context (Grenfell and similar cladding crises);
- the detailed caps and exclusions in Schedule 8 that:
  - entirely prohibit recovery in some situations; and  
  - cap it tightly in others; and
- provisions that clearly target **“historical” defects** and **existing leases** rather than only new developments.

In construing remedial statutes, English courts typically:
- give them a **purposive interpretation**, within the limits of the statutory language; and  
- avoid constructions that would readily allow evasion of the very mischief Parliament aimed to cure.

If costs incurred before commencement simply fell outside the Schedule 8 regime whenever they had not yet been fully recovered, landlords could front‑load works or time demands to escape the Act. That would punch a substantial hole in the protection, contrary to the evident legislative objective.

---

7. **Specific categories of cost in issue**

From the facts, there are two broad types of costs:

1. **Safety remediation and interim fire‑safety measures**  
   - Where those works relate to **“relevant defects”** in a relevant building and the leases are **qualifying**, Schedule 8:
     - may **wholly bar** recovery (for responsible or very wealthy landlords); or  
     - may **cap** recovery (depending on flat value and the “contribution condition”).
   - The timing of the landlord’s expenditure does **not** appear in Schedule 8 as a factor qualifying or disqualifying the protection; the focus is on:
     - nature of the defect;  
     - status of the lease; and  
     - status/wealth of the landlord group.
   - Accordingly, to the extent the works fall within the definition of remediation of “relevant defects”, the landlord **cannot rely purely on the pre‑BSA contract and LTA 1985** to recover the full historical cost.

   Any items outside Schedule 8 (e.g. costs not attributable to a “relevant defect”, or relating to non‑qualifying leases) remain governed by the leases and the LTA 1985 and may still be recoverable.

2. **Legal steps taken to facilitate or maximise service charge recovery**  
   - Schedule 8 contains specific prohibitions on passing through to leaseholders **legal and professional costs associated with establishing or enforcing liability for relevant defects**.  
   - That prohibition is again expressed without regard to when the landlord incurred those costs; it is framed in terms of what **may be demanded or paid by way of service charge**.
   - Therefore, even if ShelterCo incurred those legal expenses before commencement, it **cannot** invoke its old contractual clauses to charge them to qualifying leaseholders insofar as they fall within the statutory prohibition.

Thus, on both categories, the statutory language and scheme point to **current enforceability**, not the date of spend, as the operative concept.

---

8. **Human rights / proportionality arguments**

ShelterCo also relies on notions of unfair deprivation of property and broader economic impact. That language echoes A1P1 ECHR considerations, but in practice:

- Parliament quite clearly **intended to interfere with landlords’ economic rights** in order to protect leaseholders and the public interest in building safety.
- The BSA does not strip all value from freeholds; it reallocates part of the remediation risk.  
- The statute includes various balancing mechanisms (caps, exemptions for smaller landlords, distinctions based on property value), evidencing a structured attempt at proportionality.

In such a context, an English court is unlikely to adopt a strained interpretation to preserve landlords’ full historic charging rights where the statutory text is clear and targeted. The appropriate forum for challenging proportionality is constitutional or human‑rights litigation, not ordinary statutory construction in a service charge dispute.

---

9. **Overall evaluation**

Putting this together:

- The **text and scheme** of the BSA (particularly Schedule 8) show a deliberate intention to:
  - apply to **existing leases** and **historic defects**; and  
  - **curtail or cap** landlords’ pre‑existing contractual and statutory rights to recover remediation‑related costs, irrespective of when those costs were incurred.

- The Act’s limitations on service charges are **prospective in operation** (they govern what is recoverable from leaseholders now), even though they look back to historic defects and expenditures. That is not the kind of impermissible retrospectivity the common law presumption protects against.

- The **mischief** the BSA addresses—leaseholders being asked to fund very large historic safety remediation—would be materially undermined if landlords could sidestep it whenever works or associated legal costs happened to be incurred before commencement.

Accordingly:

- ShelterCo can still recover **some** costs:
  - in relation to non‑qualifying leases; and  
  - for items not falling within the Schedule 8 concept of “relevant defects” or the associated legal/professional costs provisions.

- But **as regards the pre‑commencement fire‑safety and remedial costs (and associated legal costs) linked to relevant defects in qualifying leases**, the BSA **does** restrict their recovery, notwithstanding otherwise valid service charge clauses and LTA 1985 rights.

On the core issue framed in the question—whether the BSA restrains recovery of those historical fire‑safety costs under the existing leases—the court should find **in favour of the Occupants**.

1. Nature of the claim and section 28 Judicature Act 1877  

Section 28 allows the *absolute* assignment of “any debt or other legal chose in action” by writing with notice to the debtor, so that the assignee can sue in his own name.

(a) The Arnext claim as a chose in action  
The claim arises from an alleged exclusive distribution agreement and from being “cut out” of a major project. That is a commercial cause of action in contract (and possibly related economic torts). Such contractual claims are, in principle, assignable as choses in action under s.28.

(b) Requirement of an *absolute* assignment  
For s.28 to allow Cameron to sue in his own name, the assignment must be:

- Absolute (not by way of charge only);  
- In writing under the hand of the assignor; and  
- With express notice to the debtor (Hayworth).

The facts as given are important. We are told Cameron:

> sought to appear as the substituted plaintiff … contending that he would prosecute the claim **to benefit the company and on his own behalf**.

That strongly suggests:

- The company did not, in substance, divest itself entirely of the beneficial interest;  
- Cameron was, at minimum, to share proceeds with the company or hold some interest for it.

If so, two consequences follow:

1. The assignment is not “absolute” in the s.28 sense (it is at best an assignment of legal title, or a partial assignment, with some beneficial interest retained or split); and  
2. On orthodox principles, where the assignment is not absolute, the assignor (Arnext) must still be joined as a party; Cameron cannot sue wholly in his own right as if Arnext had disappeared.

That immediately brings the company-representation problem back in: if Arnext remains interested in the cause of action, the Battle v. Irish Art Promotion Centre principle (that a company must be represented by a lawyer and not by a lay director/shareholder) continues to apply.

On that basis alone, the assignment does not meet the strict statutory conditions that entitle Cameron to litigate solely in his own name; s.28 is not properly engaged in the way he claims.

2. Maintenance and champerty / public policy  

Even if one assumes, for argument’s sake, that the assignment is drafted as “absolute” on its face, Irish law still controls assignments through rules of maintenance and champerty and more general abuse-of-process doctrine.

(a) The underlying principles  

Irish law still treats maintenance and champerty as torts and crimes (see e.g. Persona Digital Telephony v Minister for Public Enterprise). The core concern is:

- The “trafficking in litigation” by persons whose only genuine interest is in the proceeds of the suit, in a way liable to distort or corrupt the litigation process.

Modern authorities accept that *not all* assignments of litigation are objectionable. An assignment will generally be tolerated where:

- The assignee has a genuine pre‑existing commercial or proprietary interest in the underlying subject‑matter; and  
- The assignment is not a mere device to enable speculation in, or manipulation of, litigation.

That is why assignments to liquidators, insurers under subrogation, factoring companies (for book debts), or a party already substantively involved in the transaction are often upheld.

(b) Application to this assignment  

Here, several features raise red flags:

1. **Purpose of the assignment**: The pleaded rationale is not ordinary commercial exploitation of an asset, but to overcome:

   - The corporation’s inability to pay for legal representation;  
   - The rules preventing a non‑lawyer director/shareholder representing the company; and  
   - Potential requirements like security for costs that bite precisely because the company is impecunious.

   That is a paradigmatic example of using an assignment to *evade* procedural and public‑policy rules that would otherwise apply to the company as plaintiff.

2. **Nature of Cameron’s supposed interest**:  
   - Before the assignment, Cameron’s interest is that of a shareholder and former director: an indirect, reflective economic exposure to Arnext’s fortunes.  
   - That type of reflective interest has always been treated as distinct from a proprietary interest in the company’s specific causes of action. The company alone owns the claim.  
   - To convert that indirect interest into a direct personal claim *precisely in order to get around company‑representation and costs rules* is closer to creating than recognising a “genuine commercial interest”.

3. **Consideration and value**:  
   - We are told the claim has been put at around €11 million.  
   - The assignment is said to be for nominal value, and Cameron intends to sue “on his own behalf” as well as for the company’s benefit.  
   - A transfer of a potentially very large litigation asset for nominal consideration, timed to allow a layperson to run major commercial litigation personally, looks much more like trafficking in a cause of action than an arm’s‑length commercial disposition.

4. **Continuing benefit to the company**:  
   - If the company is to share in any recovery, then beneficial ownership remains partly with Arnext; Cameron is essentially a vehicle or front‑man for the company’s claim.  
   - That is the textbook scenario where courts say: the assignee is funding and controlling litigation substantially for the benefit of a party who cannot itself litigate in that way. That aligns squarely with the traditional worries of champerty and maintenance.

On these facts, an Irish court is very likely to characterise this as a champertous or at least an abusive assignment: an instrumental device to re‑package a corporate claim so that it can be prosecuted by someone who could not otherwise appear for the company, thereby dulling or evading the effect of security‑for‑costs, company‑representation, and creditor‑protection rules.

Champerty/public policy operate as limits on s.28: an assignment that offends them will not be given effect even if its formalities are met.  

3. Corporate representation and abuse of process  

Irish law (Battle and its progeny) is clear that:

- A limited company, as a distinct legal person, cannot ordinarily appear in person; it must act via a solicitor and, in superior courts, counsel.  
- That rule exists for reasons of orderly administration of justice, accountability for costs, and protection of other litigants and the court.

If companies could routinely assign large claims to their directors/shareholders for nominal consideration solely to allow the director to “appear in person” and avoid security for costs or other financial obligations, the corporate‑representation rule would become largely toothless in precisely the cases where it matters most (impecunious companies with speculative or high‑risk litigation).

Irish courts are generally quick to characterise such procedural end‑runs as abuses of process. The device of assignment cannot legitimately be used to achieve indirectly what the law prohibits directly: lay representation of a company and the undermining of the costs/security regime.

Thus, even apart from classic champerty analysis, a court is likely to say:

- The dominant purpose of the assignment is to evade established procedural rules;  
- That is a misuse of s.28 and of the court’s process;  
- The court will therefore refuse to recognise the substitution of Cameron as plaintiff.

4. Company law and fiduciary duties  

The claim against Hayworth is an asset of Arnext Controls and Engineering Limited. Company law imposes duties on directors:

- To act in good faith in what they reasonably believe to be the best interests of the company;  
- To avoid conflicts of interest;  
- Not to misapply or misappropriate company property, particularly for their own benefit and especially where creditors are at risk.

Key points here:

1. **Transfer at nominal value**:  
   - A potential €11 million claim transferred for nominal consideration to a former director and principal shareholder is, on its face, a related‑party transaction at a gross undervalue.  
   - At minimum, this is presumptively inconsistent with the duty to obtain proper value for a substantial corporate asset.

2. **Creditor protection**:  
   - If Arnext is in financial difficulty (as suggested by its inability to fund litigation), such a transfer removes a valuable asset from the company’s estate and from the reach of its creditors in favour of a controlling insider.  
   - That is precisely the type of disposition that insolvency and company law rules seek to prevent or unwind.

3. **Who may challenge?**  
   - Normally, internal breaches of duty render a transaction voidable at the instance of the company or a liquidator; they do not *automatically* allow a third‑party debtor to refuse to honour an assignment.  
   - However, where the transaction is also an attempt to pervert procedural rules and is, in substance, an unlawful device, a defendant is entitled to say the court should not permit the assignee to rely on it in order to sue in his own name.

Thus, company‑law principles reinforce rather than weaken the public‑policy objection. The court would be rightly concerned that:

- A large corporate asset is being stripped out for nominal value to an insider;  
- The move is engineered to obtain procedural advantages (evading company representation and possibly security for costs) while side‑stepping governance and creditor‑protection norms.

5. Balancing access to justice  

Cameron’s strongest policy argument is access to justice: if impecunious companies cannot fund legal representation, an assignment to a shareholder who will bear the risk and cost is said to be the only realistic way to vindicate a meritorious claim.

However:

- Access to justice cannot be pursued by methods that undermine other core public policies (against champerty; in favour of orderly corporate representation; in favour of creditor protection).  
- Irish courts, particularly in Persona, have been explicit that such policy questions about litigation funding and radical innovation in litigation structures are for the Oireachtas, not for judicial re‑engineering via strained applications of existing statutes.  
- There are alternative lawful mechanisms (e.g. applications to modify or manage security for costs, representation orders, or, where appropriate, third‑party funding within existing constraints) that do not involve stripping corporate assets to insiders or re‑labelling corporate claims as personal ones to circumvent procedural rules.

From an Irish court’s likely perspective, validating this assignment would indeed “open the floodgates” to similar corporate devices and would substantially erode the corporate‑representation and costs/security regimes in cases of impecunious companies. That systemic cost to the administration of justice would outweigh the individual access‑to‑justice appeal of this particular arrangement.

6. Overall conclusion  

- The assignment, as described, is not “absolute” within the meaning of s.28, because the company is still to benefit from the proceeds; thus Cameron cannot sue purely in his own name.  
- Even if it were treated as absolute in form, the transaction is contrary to public policy: it is a champertous or at least abusive attempt to traffic in a bare right to litigate and to evade settled procedural rules on company representation and security for costs.  
- Company‑law principles about fiduciary duties and creditor protection strongly militate against upholding the validity of such a transfer, especially given the nominal consideration for an enormous claimed asset and the insider nature of the transaction.

Accordingly, an Irish court should refuse to recognise Cameron as a valid assignee entitled to prosecute the claim in his own name. The assignment should be held ineffective for the purposes of substituting him as plaintiff, leaving the cause of action where it belongs: with Arnext Controls and Engineering Limited.  

In that event, Hayworth Automation’s objections succeed.

1. **Status of the 2011 regime under EU law**

- The *Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011* mandated **general and indiscriminate** retention of traffic and location data for long periods.
- In *Digital Rights Ireland* (C‑293/12) and later in *Tele2 Sverige/Watson* and related cases, the CJEU held that:
  - Blanket, non‑targeted retention of such data is incompatible with Articles 7, 8 and 11 of the Charter.
  - Access by law enforcement must be subject to **prior review by a court or an independent administrative body**, except in duly justified emergencies.
- The 2011 Act clearly lacked that “independent prior review” safeguard and provided for broad, undifferentiated retention.

So, measured against later CJEU jurisprudence, the 2011 regime is incompatible with EU law. A national court is now obliged to **disapply** the 2011 Act to the extent of that incompatibility.

However, that only answers (a) whether there was a breach of Henry Doyle’s EU‑law privacy rights, and (b) whether the retention/access regime can continue to operate. It does **not yet answer** (c) whether evidence obtained under that regime must automatically be excluded in criminal trials.

2. **Does EU law itself require exclusion of the evidence?**

Key EU‑law points:

- The CJEU has invalidated data retention frameworks and insisted on strict safeguards, but it has **not** laid down a general EU rule that all evidence obtained under defective retention laws must be excluded in criminal proceedings.
- Instead, it consistently emphasises:
  - The **supremacy** of EU law and the duty to disapply incompatible national rules.
  - The **principle of effectiveness**: national rules on evidence and procedure must not make the exercise of EU‑law rights “impossible or excessively difficult”.
  - The **principle of equivalence**: EU‑law based claims must not be treated less favourably than similar purely domestic rights claims.

Within those constraints, the CJEU generally leaves **remedies**, including exclusion of evidence, to **national procedural autonomy**, provided the overall protection of Charter rights is real and not illusory.

Accordingly:

- EU law requires acknowledgment that the 2011 Act breached Charter rights and must be brought into conformity going forward.
- It does **not** unequivocally require that all past data obtained under that regime be treated as automatically inadmissible in criminal trials, irrespective of national rules and the good‑faith reliance of investigators.

So, admissibility turns primarily on Irish law, subject to EU principles of effectiveness and equivalence.

3. **Irish exclusionary rule and unlawfully obtained evidence**

The leading modern authority is **DPP v JC [2015] IESC 31**, which restated the exclusionary rule for evidence obtained in breach of constitutional rights:

- Evidence obtained in **deliberate and conscious** violation of constitutional rights is presumptively inadmissible.
- However, evidence obtained in **good faith**, where the Gardaí reasonably believed they were acting lawfully, will **generally be admissible**, subject to the trial judge’s discretion and the requirement of a fair trial.
- The focus is on the state of mind of the investigating authorities, not on the later legal characterisation of the statute.

Here, the key considerations are:

a. **Good‑faith reliance on the 2011 Act**

- At the time of the investigation in **May 2017**, the 2011 Act was:
  - Duly enacted by the Oireachtas,
  - In force,
  - Not yet declared invalid or disapplied by any Irish court.
- Gardaí are not constitutional or EU‑law courts. It would be unrealistic, and contrary to legal certainty, to require them to override an Act of the Oireachtas on the basis of evolving and complex CJEU case law, particularly in the absence of a domestic ruling on that Act.
- Even though *Digital Rights Ireland* (2014) and *Tele2/Watson* (2016) existed, the 2011 Act remained on the statute book and had not been judicially set aside. Many Member States attempted to “salvage” or interpret national retention laws post‑*Digital Rights Ireland*; Ireland was not unique in this.

On these facts, the Gardaí were:
- Acting under an **apparently valid statute**,
- With no domestic judicial ruling that the statute was inconsistent with EU law,
- In the course of investigating a **serious firearms offence** involving a shooting.

It is very difficult to characterise their conduct as a **deliberate and conscious violation** of rights in the sense required by *JC*.

b. **Nature and seriousness of the breach**

- There is a **rights violation**: the 2011 regime, judged now against EU standards, impermissibly enabled:
  - General and indiscriminate retention, and
  - Access without independent prior authorisation.
- But in the *JC* framework, the crucial question is whether the breach was **knowingly** committed or resulted from **reckless disregard** of rights.
- Following a legislative scheme that has not yet been struck down does not ordinarily amount to such recklessness. The core constitutional and EU‑law failing lies in the **legislative design**, not in Garda bad faith.

c. **Reliability of the evidence and fairness of the trial**

- Phone metadata (cell site and call records) are objective, system‑generated data. There is no suggestion of fabrication or unreliability.
- The records are only **one component** in a broader evidential mosaic: the Lexus, its burning, convoy movements, and other circumstantial evidence.
- The defence was aware of the source and could cross‑examine, challenge inferences, and contest weight. The accused’s ability to defend himself was not impaired in any direct procedural sense by the way the records were obtained.

Under Irish law, the trial judge’s principal concern is whether admission of the evidence would render the trial **unfair**. Given:
- the seriousness of the crime,
- the objective nature of the evidence,
- the absence of deceit or oppression,
- the Gardaí’s reasonable reliance on existing legislation,

it is unlikely that admission would be seen as undermining the fairness of the trial.

4. **EU law constraints on that Irish approach**

Could EU law (effectiveness/equivalence) require a stricter approach than *JC*?

- **Equivalence**: Where constitutional rights are breached by a purely national illegality (e.g. a domestic statute later found unconstitutional), *JC* already allows admission in the absence of deliberate wrongdoing. Treating Charter breaches the same way respects equivalence: EU‑based and domestically‑based privacy rights are handled under the same exclusionary framework.
- **Effectiveness**: The defence argues that if evidence is admitted, Charter rights are hollow. That overstates the point:
  - The 2011 regime can no longer lawfully operate going forward; new legislation and practices must conform to EU law.
  - Individuals can seek declarations, damages or other civil remedies for rights violations.
  - In criminal trials, courts can and do exclude evidence where there is abuse, bad faith, or unfairness.

A rule that **always** excludes evidence obtained under a later‑invalidated retention law, even where the authorities relied in good faith on a statute, is not required by the CJEU’s case law. A rule that **sometimes** allows admission where there was good faith and no impact on trial fairness does not, by itself, render Charter protections ineffective.

5. **Balancing interests and conclusion**

Taking all this together:

- The 2011 retention/access regime is now understood to violate EU‑law privacy standards; Mr Doyle’s privacy was infringed.
- However, the Gardaí:
  - Acted under a presumptively valid statute,
  - Did not set out to evade or flout EU or constitutional rights,
  - Used the data in investigating a grave firearms offence.

Under *DPP v JC*, this points strongly towards **admission** of the phone records, subject to the judge’s assessment that the trial remains fair. There is no clear basis in Irish or EU law compelling automatic exclusion.

On these facts, an Irish court would be justified in:

- Recognising the incompatibility of the 2011 Act with EU law for future operation,
- But **admitting the already‑obtained communication records** in this prosecution, and
- Upholding the conviction.

1. **Statutory framework and what must be proved**

Under the Road Traffic Act 2010 and the associated regulations, the prosecution gets a special evidential shortcut: if it produces a statement generated by an approved breath‑analysis device, in the prescribed form and duly completed (including the requisite signatures), it is admissible as evidence of the accused’s breath alcohol concentration without calling the operator or any technical witnesses.

The essential statutory elements, in substance, are:

- An *approved device* is used.
- Two breath specimens are taken and analysed.
- The device produces two identical statements in the *prescribed form*.
- Both statements are *duly completed*, including being signed by the Garda and by the motorist.
- One statement is retained and one is furnished to the motorist.

On the facts given, all of these **substantive elements** are satisfied. The only departure is the *sequence* in which the signatures were applied.

2. **“Due completion” concerns substance, not choreography**

The defence argument is that the phrase “duly completed” (or equivalent statutory wording) imports absolute, literal compliance with *every* procedural detail, including the order in which signatures are added.

Irish courts have certainly insisted that, where legislation creates a documentary shortcut that displaces the hearsay rule and confers special evidential status, the statutory conditions must be satisfied. However, the case law distinguishes between:

- **Substantive defects**: e.g. a missing signature, absence of any required statutory statement, incorrect or missing core particulars (time, place, concentration, identity of person), use of an unapproved device, or clear non‑compliance with a condition that goes to reliability or authentication. These have been treated as failures of “due completion” that can be fatal.

- **Purely technical or formal defects**: e.g. minor clerical errors, formatting irregularities, or deviations that do not affect the reliability of the reading, the authenticity of the document, or the fairness of the process. Courts have generally refused to treat such defects as destroying admissibility, particularly where the statute does not expressly provide that such non‑compliance is fatal.

The order in which the Garda and the motorist sign is, in substance, a **formal step of authentication**, not part of the scientific measurement. Once both signatures are on the document, the evidential statement is authenticated. The measurement has been taken; the device has produced the result; the parties have attested to it.

Labeling that earlier procedural mis‑sequencing as a failure of “due completion” overextends that concept. “Due completion” should focus on whether, when the statement is tendered, it contains all required information and signatures in the prescribed form, not on the historical choreography of how it got that way.

3. **Mandatory vs directory requirements**

When deciding whether a statutory requirement is *mandatory* (non‑compliance makes the act or document a nullity) or *directory* (non‑compliance is an irregularity but not fatal), Irish courts look to:

- The **text**: Is there express language that non‑compliance invalidates the certificate or renders it inadmissible?
- The **purpose** of the provision: Is this step central to reliability/fairness, or is it administrative?
- The **consequences** of strictness: Would treating this requirement as mandatory defeat the legislative purpose by encouraging technical ambushes?

Here:

- The Act and regulations require that the statements be signed by both the Garda and the motorist and that one be furnished to the motorist. They do *not* expressly say that failure to follow the precise signing order deprives the document of its evidential status.
- The **purpose** of signatures is to authenticate the machine‑generated reading and record that the motorist has been made aware of the result and the time/place. That purpose is fully met once the document bears both signatures.
- Treating the signing order as mandatory would mean that a person whose alcohol concentration is reliably and contemporaneously measured well above the limit could escape conviction purely because the Garda invited the motorist to sign before (or after) signing himself. That outcome would cut sharply against the obvious legislative purpose of making prosecutions efficient and dependent on objective scientific evidence rather than technical traps.

These indicators heavily favour construing the signing order as **directory**. A breach is an irregularity that could be explored in cross‑examination but does not, of itself, make the document inadmissible.

4. **Absence of prejudice or unfairness**

No prejudice to Mr Carter is articulated on the facts:

- He was tested on an approved device.
- The two statements are identical and accurately reflect the machine reading.
- Both statements are signed by Garda Flynn and Mr Carter.
- There is no allegation that he was misled about the content, that his signature was obtained under misrepresentation, or that he was denied information that the procedure is designed to secure.

The rights protected by the statutory safeguards—reliability of the result, transparency of the process, and notice to the accused—have all been respected. The deviation complained of is therefore *formal*, not substantive.

Irish courts generally require some showing of **actual or potential unfairness** before treating a procedural misstep as vitiating an otherwise reliable statutory certificate or statement. Here, none is present.

5. **Avoiding hyper‑technical nullification of legislative purpose**

The legislature’s clear intent in the Road Traffic Act 2010 was to:

- Rely on objective, mechanical breath‑analysis readings; and
- Allow those readings to be proved efficiently and reliably by way of prescribed statements.

Adopting Mr Carter’s position would effectively transform the detailed regulatory scheme into a minefield, where trivial departures from sequence (even when fully documented and harmless) would nullify otherwise unimpeachable evidence. That is not consistent with contemporary Irish interpretive practice in this area, which has moved away from allowing purely technical defects to defeat the central policy of road safety legislation and the reliable proof of drink‑driving offences.

6. **Conclusion**

Because:

- All substantive statutory conditions for evidential breath statements were satisfied (proper device, two specimens, prescribed form, both signatures present, copy furnished);  
- The statute does not expressly make the signing sequence a condition of admissibility;  
- The signing order is a directory, formal requirement rather than a core safeguard of reliability or fairness; and  
- No prejudice or unfairness to Mr Carter is shown,

an Irish court should hold that the departure from the prescribed sequence of signing does **not** deprive the statements of their admissible and presumptive evidential status.

Accordingly, the Director of Public Prosecutions should prevail.

Under the Part‑time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000 (“the Regulations”), the court’s task is:

1. Is Reeves a part‑time worker with a comparable full‑time colleague?  
2. Has he been treated less favourably as regards terms of his contract or other detriment?  
3. Was that treatment “on the ground that” he is a part‑time worker?  
4. If so, can Stone Rides objectively justify the treatment?

The dispute put to you is almost entirely about step (3): does “on the ground that” require part‑time work to be the **sole** cause, or merely an **effective reason** among others?

I. The statutory wording and the Directive

Regulation 5(1) provides that a part‑time worker has the right not to be treated less favourably than a comparable full‑time worker “on the ground that the worker is a part‑time worker” unless the treatment is justified on objective grounds.

Directive 97/81, clause 4(1) of the Framework Agreement, uses the phrase “solely because they work part time”.

Two immediate points follow:

- The UK *deliberately* did **not** copy “solely” into the Regulations.  
- There is no rule that national law must mirror the Directive word‑for‑word; it must at least achieve the Directive’s minimum. Member States are free to go further and afford *greater* protection.

That freedom is explicitly recognised in EU law (e.g. now Article 153(4) TFEU and in many social directives themselves): Member States may “maintain or introduce more favourable” provisions for workers. So long as the Regulations secure at least the Directive’s standard, the UK can choose a broader test of causation.

If Parliament or the Secretary of State had wished to confine protection to cases where part‑time status was the **only** reason, the natural and obvious choice would have been to repeat “solely because”. They did not. Reading “solely” back into the text would contradict the language actually enacted.

II. The domestic discrimination law meaning of “on the ground of”

The Regulations use the classic discrimination formula: “on the ground that the worker is a part‑time worker”.

In domestic law, that phrase – “on the ground(s) of …” – has been analysed repeatedly in the context of race and sex discrimination (and later equality legislation). The House of Lords in cases such as:

- **Nagarajan v London Regional Transport** [1999] 1 WLR 425 (race discrimination), and  
- subsequent authorities applying that approach,

has made clear that:

- The “ground” of the treatment is the **reason why** the employer acted as they did.  
- There may be **multiple reasons**: some lawful, some unlawful.  
- The prohibited ground (e.g. race, sex, etc.) need not be the **sole**, or even the predominant, reason; it must be an **effective and operative cause** – a real, not trivial, influence on the decision.

That is now a settled approach for the phrase “on the ground(s) of” in UK discrimination law.

The Regulations were enacted against that background. They adopt the same wording and sit within the same general family of anti‑discrimination measures. Absent clear indication to the contrary in the legislation itself, the courts will read “on the ground that the worker is a part‑time worker” in the **same** way: part‑time status must be an operative cause of the less favourable treatment, but need not be the only cause.

III. Interaction with Directive 97/81

Stone Rides argues that because the Directive uses “solely because”, the domestic Regulations must be construe d to the same, stricter standard. That does not follow.

1. **Conforming interpretation has limits.**  
UK courts must, so far as possible, interpret implementing legislation consistently with a Directive (the *Marleasing* principle). But that duty:

- cannot justify **rewriting** clear domestic wording, or  
- adopting a meaning directly contrary to the statutory text and scheme.

Here, the domestic choice to omit “solely” and to use the familiar “on the ground that” formula is clear and deliberate. Interpreting “on the ground that” as **“solely because”** would be to add a restriction Parliament/the Secretary of State consciously left out.

2. **Floor, not ceiling.**  
Clause 4(1)’s “solely because” sets the *minimum* content of EU protection: at least those who are treated less favourably solely because they work part‑time must be protected. It does *not* prevent a Member State from:

- protecting workers where part‑time status is one of several effective reasons, or  
- going further in any other way favourable to workers.

Indeed, to insist that the Regulations contain a “sole reason only” test would invert the normal EU principle: it would treat the Directive as a ceiling, not a floor.

3. **Purposive reading of the Directive.**  
The Framework Agreement’s objective is to prevent structural disadvantage to part‑time workers, who are disproportionately women and often in more precarious work. A “sole reason” test is so narrow that it would seriously undercut that goal: employers would almost always be able to point to some additional commercial or administrative rationale – “cost saving”, “revenue generation”, “market practice” – alongside part‑time status and thus escape liability.

By contrast, reading the Regulations as prohibiting less favourable treatment where part‑time status is an effective reason – subject to objective justification – aligns with both:

- the Directive’s purpose, and  
- the established structure of UK discrimination law.

There is nothing in EU law that requires the UK to adopt a weaker standard than it has chosen.

IV. Application of the causation test to the facts

On the assumptions given, the core factual points are:

- All drivers paid the same “circuit fee” for access to Stone Rides’ booking system.  
- That flat fee consumes a **larger proportion of earnings and work opportunities for part‑time drivers** than for full‑time drivers.  
- Both sides accept that Reeves’ **part‑time status was a factor** in how he was treated, although they dispute whether it was the sole basis.  
- Stone Rides says the principal reason for the fee is commercial: raising revenue and mirroring sector practice.

The legal analysis is then:

1. **Less favourable treatment.**  
Although the nominal fee is the same, its effect relative to work done and earnings is significantly worse for part‑time workers. Under the Regulations, the comparison is not confined to facially identical clauses; the court may look at whether, in substance, the part‑time worker is placed at a disadvantage in employment conditions vis‑à‑vis a comparable full‑timer.

On the facts presented, the circuit fee **operates** in a materially less favourable way for part‑time drivers. It is a detriment linked to their conditions of work and access to work.

2. **“On the ground that he is a part‑time worker.”**  
The agreed position is that Reeves’ part‑time status was a **causal factor** in the treatment complained of. That is precisely what the “mixed motive” line of case law addresses: where there are both commercial reasons (raising revenue) and status‑related reasons (structuring or applying the scheme in a way that particularly burdens part‑timers).

Given the proper interpretation of the Regulations:

- Reeves does **not** need to show that Stone Rides charged – or structured – the fee *only* because he works part‑time.  
- He needs to show that his being part‑time was **one effective and operative reason** for the less favourable treatment.

On the assumed facts, that threshold is met: the way the uniform fee impacts access to work makes part‑time status an operative reason for the disadvantage, even if Stone Rides was also seeking to raise revenue.

3. **Stone Rides’ revenue rationale.**  
The fact that Stone Rides can point to a commercial aim does **not** negate discrimination if part‑time status also materially influenced how the scheme was set up or applied. That is classic mixed‑motive territory: the existence of a legitimate financial objective may be relevant at the **objective justification** stage, but it does not erase causal connection at the liability stage.

V. Objective justification

Under regulation 5(2), even if there is less favourable treatment on the ground of part‑time status, the employer can escape liability if it shows the treatment is **justified on objective grounds**.

A lawful justification requires:

- a legitimate aim (for example, raising revenue to fund the booking system), and  
- means that are appropriate and necessary, i.e. proportionate, to that aim.

Stone Rides’ aim is plainly legitimate. The difficulty is proportionality. A uniform flat fee that bears no relation to hours worked predictably places a heavier burden on part‑timers than full‑timers. There are obvious less discriminatory alternatives – e.g. a pro‑rata fee based on hours, bookings, or earnings.

Without evidence that such alternatives were impracticable or would undermine the business model, a tribunal would be likely to find that imposing a single undifferentiated fee was **not** the least discriminatory means of achieving the revenue goal. On the facts as presented (which do not show any compelling necessity for the flat structure), Stone Rides would struggle to discharge the burden of objective justification.

VI. Conclusion

Legally, the Regulations do **not** impose a “sole reason” test. The phrase “on the ground that the worker is a part‑time worker” should be construed consistently with domestic discrimination law as requiring that part‑time status be an effective and operative cause of the less favourable treatment, not the only cause. That approach is compatible with, and indeed furthers, Directive 97/81, which sets a minimum standard that the UK was free to exceed.

On the facts given, Reeves’ part‑time status was an operative factor in his disadvantage under the circuit fee scheme, and Stone Rides’ general revenue rationale does not displace that. Nor, on the information provided, is the flat fee structure objectively justified when fairer, less discriminatory mechanisms are available.

Accordingly, an English court should find for the claimant.
